summary: Instagram is doing the real work: almost every Hindi video gets 1,200+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly stay under 50 views. The best videos are short, surprising 'X doesn't do what you think' statements about hands-on robots and sensors (gyro robot, clap switch, line follower, mic). Everyday-tech explainers about taps, doors, smoke alarms and lifts, and the English Arduino video, get little attention.
winningPattern: Hindi videos about a robot or a hobby-circuit that makers can build (gyro, clap switch, line follower, IR obstacle robot, mic). The hook is a surprising 'it doesn't do what you think' claim, such as 'Without X this robot falls' or 'Clap switch listens to noise, not clapping'. Titles are short Hinglish with a bold claim and a robot or clap emoji, posted on Instagram first. The best ones also drive saves and shares, a sign that people want to keep or send them.
doMore: Make robot and maker-project videos (gyro, line follower, clap switch, obstacle avoidance) with a visible 'before vs after' demo in the first 2 seconds
Open with a bold, counter-intuitive claim like 'X can't see/hear, yet it...' instead of a question
Add a save or share prompt like 'Save this for your next project' since saves and shares signal strong interest
Post to Instagram first and test 2-3 YouTube-specific titles and thumbnails to see why YT lags
Turn the top hits into series (Part 2: what happens if you remove the sensor?)
stopDoing: Question-style titles about public devices (mall door, washroom tap, lift, street light) that got the weakest views
Publishing near-duplicate topics (two smoke detector videos, two automatic tap videos, two IR sensor videos) within days of each other
Mixing in English narration until Hindi on YouTube is working
